/short-term-property-management/.html:
Short-term property management is the day-to-day running of a property let out for stays of a few nights to a few weeks — typically via platforms like Airbnb and Booking.com — rather than to a single long-term tenant. Ichiban Stays provides short term let management for landlords across the UK and handles every part of that process, end to end.

You may also see this called short let management or short term rental management. If you plan to let through Airbnb specifically, see our Airbnb management in London page.

What Short Let Management Involves

  • Listing creation and optimisation across booking platforms
  • Dynamic pricing to reflect demand, seasonality and local events
  • Guest communication, check-in and check-out
  • Professional cleaning and linen changes between every stay
  • Ongoing maintenance and property upkeep
  • Monitoring compliance with current short-let regulations

Short-Term vs Long-Term Letting

Short lets generally offer higher gross income potential than a single long-term tenancy, because nightly rates for short stays are typically higher than the pro-rated equivalent of a monthly rent — though they also come with higher operating involvement (turnover, cleaning, variable occupancy) and clearer regulatory limits in London specifically. A managed service is what makes the higher-income model realistic without turning it into a second job. Read more in our guide to Airbnb vs traditional tenancy for landlords.

Short-Let Regulations

London currently caps whole-property short lets at 90 nights per calendar year without planning permission. Outside London, short-let rules are set locally and vary by council and nation, so we check the position for your property before it goes live. We keep this front of mind when managing every property. Full detail: short-term rental regulations in London.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does short let management include?

Listing your property, dynamic pricing with PriceLabs, guest communication, check-in and check-out, cleaning between stays, maintenance, compliance and regular reporting. Ichiban Stays handles all of it end to end.

Is there an upfront fee?

No. There are no upfront fees to get started. We explain our management fee clearly in your free consultation, before you commit to anything.

How do you handle the 90-night rule?

We track nights for you and plan around the limit, for example by mixing short stays with longer serviced accommodation bookings. Our guide to the Airbnb 90-day rule in London explains the rules in full.

Do I need to be available during guest stays?

No. Your dedicated manager and our team handle guest communication, check-ins, check-outs and any issues during a stay.

How do I find out what my property could earn?

Book a free, no-obligation property assessment. We give you a realistic estimate of short-let income compared with a long let.

Is Short-Term Management Right for Your Property?

It depends on the property, its location and your goals as a landlord. Get a free income projection and we'll give you a straight answer, based on your specific property.

What Is Serviced Accommodation?

Serviced accommodation is fully furnished, professionally managed accommodation let on a flexible basis — typically to business travellers, relocating professionals and guests staying longer than a typical holiday visit, rather than short tourist stays alone.

How Serviced Accommodation Differs From a Standard Short Let

  • Guests tend to stay longer on average — days to weeks or months, rather than a single weekend
  • A stronger focus on consistency, presentation and hotel-style standards
  • Often used for corporate relocation, contractors and extended-stay travellers

Our Serviced Accommodation Management Services

  • Furnishing and presentation standards
  • Guest vetting, communication and stay management
  • Cleaning, restocking and property upkeep between stays
  • Pricing appropriate to the extended-stay and corporate market
  • Compliance and safety standards

Who Stays in Serviced Accommodation

Serviced accommodation attracts guests who need a home rather than a hotel room for a while:

  • Corporate guests and project teams on assignments of several weeks
  • Professionals relocating to a new city while they look for a long-term home
  • Contractors, consultants and NHS staff working near a particular site
  • Families staying longer, for example during building work or a hospital stay

These guests value a reliable standard, a quiet building and a proper kitchen and workspace. They also tend to treat the property with care.

Why Landlords Choose It

  • Steadier occupancy. Longer stays mean fewer gaps and fewer turnovers than weekend tourist bookings.
  • Lower wear and tear. Fewer check-ins and check-outs mean less cleaning and less disruption for neighbours.
  • Flexibility. Unlike a standard tenancy, you're not tied into a 12-month agreement.
  • Fits local rules. Longer stays can help a property work around the 90-night limit on short lets. We'll confirm how this applies to your property.

How We Run It

We price for the extended-stay and corporate market with PriceLabs, and run operations on our in-house property management software. Each property has a dedicated manager, and our team brings more than 20 years of experience in hospitality. You get regular reporting and payouts, with no upfront fees to get started.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between serviced accommodation and a short let?

Serviced accommodation usually means longer stays, from days to weeks or months, with a stronger focus on hotel-style standards. Guests are often corporate travellers or people relocating, rather than weekend tourists.

Who books serviced accommodation?

Corporate guests and project teams, professionals relocating for work, contractors and NHS staff working near a particular site, and families who need a home for a while.

Does my property need to be furnished?

Yes, serviced accommodation is let fully furnished. We advise on furnishing and presentation so the property meets guest expectations.

Can serviced accommodation help with the 90-night rule?

Longer stays of several months are generally treated as ordinary residential lettings rather than short lets, so they can help a property earn beyond 90 short-let nights. We confirm how this applies to your property and borough.

Is there an upfront fee?

No. There are no upfront fees to get started, and we explain our management fee in your free consultation.

Is Serviced Accommodation Right for Your Property?

Well-located properties near transport links, business districts or hospitals tend to perform particularly well as serviced accommodation. Get a free income projection and we'll advise honestly on whether serviced accommodation or standard short-let management is the better fit for your specific property.

/airbnb-vs-traditional-tenancy-for-landl.seoTitle: Airbnb vs Long-Term Rental After the Renters' Rights Act
/airbnb-vs-traditional-tenancy-for-landl.description: Airbnb vs long-term rental in London after the Renters' Rights Act: what changed on 1 May 2026, how it affects landlords, and when short lets make sense.
/airbnb-vs-traditional-tenancy-for-landl.html:
For London landlords deciding how to let a property, the choice often comes down to a standard long-term tenancy or a short-term/Airbnb-style let. Both are legitimate strategies — the right one depends on the property and what the landlord wants from it.

What Changed for London Landlords on 1 May 2026

The Renters' Rights Act received Royal Assent on 27 October 2025, and its main tenancy changes in England took effect on 1 May 2026. For a landlord weighing up a long-term let against Airbnb, these are the changes that matter most:

  • Section 21 has gone. Landlords can no longer end a tenancy with a "no-fault" eviction notice. To get a property back you now need a specific legal ground, such as selling or moving in, and notice periods apply.
  • Tenancies are periodic. Fixed-term assured shorthold tenancies have been replaced by rolling tenancies. Tenants can leave with two months' notice.
  • Rent increases are limited. Rent can be raised once a year through a formal section 13 notice with two months' notice, and rent review clauses no longer apply.
  • Rent in advance is restricted to one month at the start of a tenancy, and landlords must not invite or accept offers above the advertised rent.
  • Pets: tenants can ask to keep a pet, and a landlord must not refuse unreasonably.

More measures, including a private landlord database and an ombudsman scheme, are due to follow in later phases.

How the Act Changes the Airbnb vs Long-Term Rental Decision

A long-term let is still the lowest-effort way to let a property. What has changed is control. Once a tenant moves in, it is harder and slower to get the property back, and rent can only rise once a year.

Short-term and holiday lets work differently. Guests book for a set stay, and a genuine holiday let is generally not an assured tenancy, so the new tenancy rules do not apply to it in the same way. You keep control of the calendar and can block dates for your own use or a planned sale. Short lets bring their own rules instead, above all London's 90-night limit for whole homes. Take legal advice on your own arrangement if you are unsure which rules apply.

That is why some London landlords are now looking again at short lets and serviced accommodation, often combining the two so the property earns all year without breaking the 90-night limit.

Traditional (Long-Term) Tenancy

  • Stable, predictable monthly rent
  • Lower day-to-day involvement — one tenant, one relationship
  • No 90-night limit, but since 1 May 2026 tenancies are rolling, section 21 has ended and rent can only rise once a year
  • Less flexibility if the landlord wants to use the property themselves occasionally

Short-Term / Airbnb-Style Letting

  • Generally higher gross income potential than an equivalent long-term rent, particularly for well-located properties
  • Significantly more operational work: guest management, cleaning between every stay, dynamic pricing
  • Subject to specific regulation in London — currently a 90-night annual cap on whole-property short lets without planning permission (see our regulations guide)
  • Income varies with demand and seasonality, rather than being fixed

Which Is More Profitable?

Short-term letting can generate higher income than long-term letting for the right property in the right location — but that gap narrows once cleaning, management time, void periods and compliance are accounted for. This is exactly the calculation a management service is built to optimise, since the operational cost of doing it well is spread across many properties rather than falling entirely on one landlord.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does the Renters' Rights Act apply to Airbnb lets?

The Act's main changes are aimed at assured tenancies, where someone lives in the property as their home. Genuine holiday and short-term lets are generally not assured tenancies, so they are treated differently. London's 90-night rule for whole-home short lets still applies.

Can I switch from a long-term tenant to short lets?

Only once the tenancy has ended lawfully. Since section 21 was abolished, that means the tenant gives notice or you use one of the legal possession grounds. Plan the switch around the tenancy, not the other way round.

Is serviced accommodation a middle ground?

For many London properties, yes. Longer stays for corporate guests, contractors and people relocating can fill the nights that short lets cannot use under the 90-night rule. Read how short-term let management works to compare.

/short-term-rental-regulations-london/.html:
Short-let regulation changes periodically — this page reflects the position as understood in 2026. Always confirm current requirements with your local council before letting a property short-term.

The Airbnb 90-Day Rule in London

In Greater London, letting an entire property on a short-term basis is currently capped at 90 nights per calendar year without planning permission. This applies per property, per year, across all booking platforms combined — not per platform individually. Rooms let while the host is present are generally treated differently from whole-property lets.

This is often called the Airbnb 90-day rule, although it applies to every platform. Airbnb automatically limits entire-home listings in London to 90 nights a year unless the host confirms they have planning permission.

How to Get Around the Airbnb 90-Day Rule Legally

There is no loophole, but there are legal ways to earn from a London property beyond 90 short-let nights:

  • Apply for planning permission. With approval for change of use, the cap no longer applies. Requirements vary by borough.
  • Add longer stays. Stays of several months, such as corporate lets and relocations, are generally treated as ordinary residential lettings rather than short lets. Mixing these with short stays can keep a property earning all year. Check how your council treats them.
  • Let a room while you live there. The cap applies to letting an entire home, not a room in a home you live in.
  • Plan your nights. Use the 90 nights for your highest-earning dates, and fill the rest with longer lets.

Ichiban Stays tracks nights for landlords and plans around the limit. See our Airbnb management in London service.

Planning Permission Above 90 Nights

Once a property is let short-term for more than 90 nights in a calendar year, most London councils treat this as a change of use requiring planning permission, rather than ordinary residential letting. Approval isn't automatic and requirements vary by borough.

Enforcement Varies by Borough

How actively this is enforced differs across London — central boroughs with high housing demand tend to apply more scrutiny, often triggered by resident complaints as much as proactive monitoring.

Changes on the Horizon

A mandatory national short-let registration scheme, and a proposed dedicated "C5" planning use class for short-term lets, have both been discussed by government but were not yet in force as of mid-2026. Landlords should keep an eye on official guidance rather than relying on any one article — including this one — as the current state of play can change.

Short-Let Rules Outside London

The 90-night limit only applies in Greater London. Elsewhere in the UK, the rules depend on where your property is:

  • England: there is no nightly cap outside London, but your mortgage, lease and insurance must allow short lets, and some councils treat a home let mostly to short-stay guests as a change of use that needs planning permission. A national registration scheme for short-term lets is expected to be fully running by March 2027. See our guides for Manchester, Birmingham, Liverpool, Leeds and Bristol.
  • Scotland: every short-term let needs a licence from the council before it takes bookings. The whole of Edinburgh is also a short-term let control area, where letting a whole property that is not your main home usually needs planning permission, and Edinburgh's 5% visitor levy starts on 24 July 2026. Glasgow's visitor levy starts on 25 January 2027.
  • Wales: a national register of visitor accommodation is being introduced, councils can add a visitor levy, and self-catering properties must meet letting thresholds to be rated for business rates. See our Cardiff guide.

We check the rules for your specific property before it goes live. See all the areas we cover.

What This Means in Practice

A managed service should be actively tracking a property's night count and compliance position, not leaving that to the landlord to monitor manually. This is a standard part of how we manage every property at Ichiban Stays.

For more background, see the London Assembly's coverage of short-term letting regulation: london.gov.uk. For your own property specifically, talk to our team about how we handle compliance.

/property-management-fees-london/.html:
If you are thinking about letting a property in London or elsewhere in the UK as a short let, the management fee is one of the first questions you will ask. This guide explains how property management fees in the UK and London are usually structured, what a fee should include, which costs sit on top of it, and how to compare quotes fairly.

How Short-Let Management Fees Are Usually Charged

Most short-let and Airbnb management companies in London and across the UK charge a percentage of the income your property earns, rather than a fixed monthly fee. If the property earns nothing in a month, the manager earns nothing either, so your interests are aligned.

The two numbers to check in any quote are the percentage itself and what it is a percentage of:

  • Gross booking revenue: the total the guest pays for the stay, sometimes including cleaning fees.
  • Net rental income: the room revenue after items such as cleaning fees or platform charges are taken out.

The same headline percentage can cost you noticeably more if it is charged on gross revenue rather than net income, so always ask.

Why Published Fees Are Hard to Compare

Few managers publish their full pricing, and those that do rarely quote like for like. One company's rate may be a percentage of gross booking revenue, including cleaning fees, while another's is a percentage of net income after platform and cleaning costs. Some quote a lower headline rate and then charge separately for onboarding, photography, linen, restocking or each reservation.

How to Compare Quotes Fairly

Choosing a company for property management is one of the biggest decisions a London landlord makes. The right manager protects your property, keeps it earning and saves you hours every week. What Does a Property Management Company Do?

A property management company runs your rental property day to day on your behalf. For a short let or serviced apartment in London, that usually means:

  • Handling guest messages, vetting and check-in

  • Keeping the property compliant, including London's 90-night rule
  • Reporting on bookings, income and costs

For a full breakdown, read what a property management company does for landlords.

Is a Property Manager the Same as a Landlord?

No. The landlord owns the property and keeps the legal responsibilities that come with it. A property manager acts for the landlord under an agreement, doing the day-to-day work the landlord chooses to hand over. You stay the owner and decision-maker; the manager runs the operation.

How to Choose the Right Property Management Company: Essential Tips

1. Check They Specialise in Your Type of Letting

Long-term lettings, short lets and serviced accommodation are different businesses. A firm that mainly finds long-term tenants may not have the pricing tools, cleaning teams or guest support a short let needs. Ask what share of their portfolio is the same type of letting as yours.

2. Ask for Their Local Knowledge

Demand in London changes from one area to the next. A good manager should explain who books in your area, how rates move through the year, and whether a short let, serviced accommodation or a standard tenancy would earn more for your property.

3. Understand Exactly How Fees Work

Most short-let managers charge a percentage of the income your property earns. Ask what the percentage is charged on, gross booking revenue or net income, and what sits outside it, such as setup, cleaning or maintenance. Our guide to property management fees in London covers this in detail.

4. Check Their Professional Protections

In England, letting and property management agents must belong to a government-approved redress scheme, and agents who hold client money must be members of a client money protection scheme. Ask which schemes a company belongs to and whether they apply to the service you are buying. Rules differ between long-term tenancies and holiday lets, so a good firm will explain clearly.

5. Ask How They Handle the 90-Night Rule

Whole-home short lets in London are limited to 90 nights a year without planning permission. A good property management firm tracks your nights and has a plan for the rest of the year, for example longer serviced accommodation stays. Read our guide to the 90-day rule.

6. Look at Communication and Reporting

Ask who your contact will be, how quickly they reply, and how often you get reports. A dedicated manager who knows your property is worth more than a general inbox.

7. Read the Property Management Agreement Carefully

The agreement sets out what the company does, what you pay and how either side can end it. Before signing, check:

  • The services included and anything charged separately
  • The notice period and any minimum term
  • Who pays for repairs, and the spending limit before they need your approval
  • How and when you receive your income
  • Insurance responsibilities on both sides
  • What happens to your listings, photos and reviews if you leave

8. Ask for an Income Projection for Your Property

A serious company should give you a realistic projection for your specific property, not an area average. Be wary of promises that sound too good to be true.

What Is Guaranteed Rent?

With guaranteed rent, a company agrees to pay you a fixed monthly rent for a set term. The company then runs the property, often as serviced accommodation or short lets for business travellers, relocating professionals and visitors. You receive the agreed amount every month, whether the property is fully booked or quiet.

The company takes on the booking risk, the guests, cleaning and the day-to-day running. In return, the guaranteed figure is usually lower than the property might earn in a strong year if you kept the income yourself.

How Guaranteed Rent Works in London

  1. Assessment: the company looks at your property’s location, size, condition and nearby demand.
  2. Offer: you receive a monthly rent figure and a proposed term.
  3. Agreement: both sides sign a written agreement covering rent, term, bills, repairs and condition.
  4. Set-up: the property is prepared for guests, with photography, listings, furnishing and linen as needed.
  5. Monthly payments: you receive the agreed rent on the agreed date for the length of the term.

Guaranteed Rent and London’s 90-Night Rule

In London, an entire home can only be let as short-term accommodation for up to 90 nights a year without planning permission. A responsible guaranteed rent operator plans around this from day one, for example by combining short stays with longer serviced accommodation bookings for corporate and relocation guests. Ask any company how they will stay within the rule for your property. Read our full guide to the 90-day rule in London.

Guaranteed Rent vs Other Options

The Pros and Cons

Advantages

  • A predictable monthly income, which helps with mortgage payments and planning
  • No void periods, tenant-finding or guest management
  • Regular cleaning and checks, so problems are spotted early

Things to weigh up

  • The guaranteed figure is usually below the property’s best-case short-let income
  • You are relying on the company to pay on time and look after the property, so choosing the right partner matters
  • Your lease, mortgage and insurance must allow the arrangement

What to Check Before You Sign

  • Who the company is: how long they have operated, who runs it and how they manage properties
  • Term and break clauses: how long the agreement lasts and how it can end
  • Payment terms: the payment date, and what happens if a payment is late
  • Bills: who pays council tax, utilities, broadband and insurance
  • Repairs and condition: who covers which repairs, and how the property is returned, backed by an inventory
  • Consents: whether your lease, freeholder, mortgage lender and insurer allow it
  • Compliance: how the company will handle the 90-night rule, safety certificates and building rules

Always take independent legal advice before signing a guaranteed rent agreement.

Is Guaranteed Rent Right for You?

Guaranteed rent suits landlords who value certainty over the highest possible income, such as those covering a mortgage, living abroad, or who simply do not want any involvement. If you would rather keep the full upside of short-let income, full management may suit you better. Many landlords compare both before deciding.

This varies by agreement. Many guaranteed rent agreements have the operator cover utilities and running costs, but always check exactly what your agreement says.

“How much can my London flat earn on short let?” is the first question most landlords ask us. The honest answer is that it depends on a handful of factors you can measure. What Decides How Much Your Property Can Earn

  • Location: distance to the sights, business districts, hospitals, universities and transport. Central zones and well-connected neighbourhoods such as Mayfair, Covent Garden, Kensington and Canary Wharf attract the widest range of guests.
  • Size and layout: the number of bedrooms, bathrooms and how many guests it sleeps comfortably.
  • Presentation: furnishing, photography and cleanliness have a direct effect on nightly rates and reviews.
  • Seasonality and events: summer, Christmas, conferences, concerts and sporting events push demand and prices up.
  • Pricing: nightly rates that follow demand day by day earn more than one fixed price.
  • The 90-night rule: in London, an entire home can only be let short-term for up to 90 nights a year without planning permission, so the mix of short and longer stays matters.

How to Estimate Your Short-Let Income

A simple way to estimate short-let income is:

Average nightly rate × nights booked = gross booking income

Then subtract your costs (see below) to reach your net income. To make the estimate realistic:

  1. Find comparable listings: look for properties near you with the same number of bedrooms and a similar standard, and note their nightly rates across different months.
  2. Be realistic about nights booked: allow for quieter months, and remember the 90-night limit for whole-home short lets in London.
  3. Add longer stays: corporate and relocation lets of 90 consecutive nights or more fall outside the short-let limit and can fill the rest of the year at different rates.
  4. Subtract every cost: estimates that ignore cleaning, platform fees and bills look better than real life.

Costs to Allow For

  • Booking platform fees
  • Cleaning and laundry between stays
  • Utilities, broadband, TV licence and council tax
  • Insurance designed for short lets
  • Furnishing, linen, consumables and replacements
  • Maintenance and safety checks, such as gas and electrical safety
  • Management, if you use a management company

Read our guide to property management fees in the UK and London for how management charges work.

Short Let vs Long Let: How to Compare

To compare fairly, put the net figures side by side:

  • Long let: monthly rent × 12, less letting fees, void periods, repairs and any bills you cover.
  • Short let: gross booking income from short and longer stays, less all the costs above.

Short lets can earn more than a long let in the right location, but income varies month to month and needs active management. If you want a fixed income instead, guaranteed rent pays an agreed amount every month. Our guide to Airbnb vs traditional tenancy covers the trade-offs in more detail.

Ways to Increase Your Short-Let Income

  • Invest in professional photography and a well-written listing
  • Use dynamic pricing, such as PriceLabs, so rates follow demand
  • List on more than one platform, such as Airbnb and Booking.com
  • Reply to guests quickly and keep cleaning standards high to protect reviews
  • Plan your 90 nights for the busiest dates, and fill the rest with longer stays
  • Add the details business guests look for: fast Wi-Fi, a desk and flexible check-in

It varies widely with location, presentation and the time of year. The most reliable answer comes from comparing similar listings near your property and allowing for every cost, or from a free property-specific projection.

It limits how many nights a whole home can be let short-term each year without planning permission. Stays of 90 consecutive nights or more do not count towards the limit, so many landlords combine their short-let nights with longer corporate or relocation lets.

It can be in the right location with good management, but income is less predictable and costs are higher. Compare net figures for both before deciding.

  • Scotland: short-term lets need a licence from the local council, and some areas, such as Edinburgh, are short-term let control areas where planning permission may also be needed.
  • Wales: registration and a visitor levy are being introduced, and whether a holiday let pays council tax or business rates depends on how many days it is available and actually let each year.
  • London: an entire home can be let short-term for up to 90 nights a year without planning permission. Read our guide to the 90-day rule in London.
